title: Levitical Cities and Cities of Refuge
summary: God commands Israel to give the Levites forty-eight cities with surrounding pasturelands, spread throughout the tribes. Six of them are to be cities of refuge, where someone who kills another person unintentionally may flee from the avenger of blood and live safely until the death of the high priest. The chapter distinguishes murder from accidental killing, requires more than one witness, forbids ransom for a murderer, and warns that bloodshed pollutes the land where the LORD dwells.
story: The last chapters of Numbers prepare Israel for life in the land. Chapter 34 drew its borders; this chapter provides for the Levites, the tribe set apart to serve at the tabernacle, who were counted separately in the census because they would receive no territory of their own (26:62). It also addresses one of the most dangerous problems of settled life: what happens when one person kills another. The cities of refuge were already anticipated in Exodus 21:13, and they are taken up again in Deuteronomy 19 and established in Joshua 20, where they are named. The Levitical cities are listed in Joshua 21. The chapter's closing words, that the LORD dwells among the Israelites, frame the whole law.
historical:
The Levites were scattered throughout Israel by design. Their cities would be drawn from every tribe in proportion to its size (verse 8), so that the tribe responsible for teaching the law and serving at the sanctuary would live among all the people. Joshua 21 lists forty-eight such cities, and some have been identified with known sites, though scholars debate whether the list reflects the time of Joshua or a later period such as the united monarchy. Joshua 20 names the six cities of refuge: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (Hebron) in Judah on the west side of the Jordan; and Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan on the east. They were spread so that no one would be far from one.

In Israel, as across the ancient Near East, there was no police force to investigate killings. Justice for a death depended heavily on the victim's family, and the avenger of blood was a relative with the duty of pursuing the killer. The cities of refuge limited that system, making sure that a killer faced trial before the community before any punishment was carried out.
cultural:
The avenger of blood (goel) was the nearest male relative of the victim, the same word used for the kinsman-redeemer who bought back family land or freed a relative from slavery (Leviticus 25) and who married Ruth (Ruth 3 and 4). His role was to restore what the family had lost, and in a killing that meant pursuing the killer. The law channels this family duty into a legal process. A person who killed someone could flee to a city of refuge; the assembly would judge whether the act was murder or accident, using evidence such as the weapon, any prior hostility, and intent. A murderer was handed over to die. An accidental killer was protected but had to stay in the city until the high priest died. The high priest's death seems to have marked a turning point after which the manslayer could return home, and many interpreters see in it an atoning significance, as if the death of the anointed priest settled the matter of the blood that had been shed.

Some other ancient law collections, such as the Hittite laws, allowed killing to be settled by compensation. Israel's law refuses ransom for a murderer (verse 31), because human life, made in God's image (Genesis 9:6), cannot be bought off.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-8 give instructions for the Levitical cities, including the measurement of their pasturelands (the two measurements, a thousand and two thousand cubits, have puzzled interpreters, and several ways of reconciling them have been proposed). Verses 9-34 give the law of refuge, organized as case law. A series of examples defines murder: striking with an iron object, a deadly stone, a wooden weapon, or pushing or striking out of hatred. A contrasting series defines accidental killing: suddenly, without hostility, without looking. Procedural rules follow, and the chapter ends with theological reasons: bloodshed pollutes the land, and the land must not be defiled “where I dwell.” The repeated phrase “the murderer must surely be put to death” gives the first series a strong, grave rhythm.

outline.t: Six cities of refuge for unintentional killers
Cases of accidental killing and the high priest's death
Witnesses, no ransom, and the pollution of the land

doctrines.note: The chapter treats human life as so valuable that a murderer's life cannot be ransomed, while it also protects those who kill without intent. Both rulings rest on the dignity of the person made in God's image.

The law distinguishes intention from accident, requires more than one witness, and gives the accused a trial before the community. It restrains private vengeance and puts justice in the hands of a public process.
Bloodshed pollutes the land, and the land must not be defiled because the LORD dwells among his people. Justice is not merely social order but part of keeping a holy God's dwelling clean.

The chapter states that no atonement can be made for the land on which blood is shed except by the blood of the one who shed it, and it ties the manslayer's release to the death of the high priest. Both point to the costliness of dealing with bloodguilt.

words.note: Miqlat, refuge. The word, from a root meaning to take in or receive, is used in the Old Testament only for these cities of refuge. It describes a place that receives and protects someone in danger. The idea of God as refuge runs through the Psalms, though with different Hebrew words.

Ga'al, here in the sense of avenging. The goel of blood is the family member responsible for pursuing the killer. The same root elsewhere describes a kinsman who redeems land or people, and it is used of God as Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 41:14). Its basic idea is a family member acting to restore what was lost.

Ratsach, to kill or murder. It is the verb used in the commandment “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). In this chapter it is used both of murder and of accidental killing, and the context clarifies which is meant. The law's task is to distinguish between them.
Chanaph, to pollute or profane. The land itself becomes polluted when innocent blood is shed and not dealt with. The prophets use the word for the land defiled by Israel's sins (Jeremiah 3:1-2).

christ: Hebrews draws on the language of refuge when it says that “we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged”, a hope that “enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:18-20). Many Christian readers have seen the cities of refuge as a picture of Christ, the place of safety for those who flee from judgment, and the release that came with the death of the high priest as a picture of the freedom won by the death of Christ, the great high priest. These are typological readings, not claims that Numbers predicts them. The chapter's insistence that blood pollutes the land and can only be dealt with by blood also stands behind the New Testament's language about Jesus' blood, which “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).
questions: The cities of refuge protected those who killed without intending to. What does this law teach about the importance of motive and intention in judging wrongdoing?
Why do you think God required the manslayer to stay in the city of refuge until the high priest's death, rather than simply setting him free after trial?
The chapter says bloodshed pollutes the land. How might injustice affect not only individuals but a whole community and place?
